title: Major Energy Investments Bring Jobs and Growth to Louisiana - Avoyelles Today
description:
Louisiana continues to strengthen its role as a leader in energy and industrial development as two major projects totaling nearly $5 billion in investment have recently been announced for the state.
Shintech Louisiana, LLC revealed plans for a $3.4 billion expansion of its manufacturing operations in Iberville Parish.

text:
Louisiana continues to strengthen its role as a leader in energy and industrial development as two major projects totaling nearly $5 billion in investment have recently been announced for the state.

Shintech Louisiana, LLC revealed plans for a $3.4 billion expansion of its manufacturing operations in Iberville Parish. The project will include construction of a second ethylene unit along with a fourth chlor-alkali and vinyl chloride monomer production unit at the company’s existing facility in Plaquemine.

Construction will occur in phases, with the first phase expected to be completed by 2030.

The expansion is expected to create 163 new direct jobs with an average annual salary of $117,329, which is about 42 percent higher than the average wage in Iberville Parish. The company will also retain 725 existing positions. Louisiana Economic Development estimates the project could generate an additional 655 indirect jobs, bringing the total potential job impact to more than 800 jobs across the Capital Region.

Governor Jeff Landry said the investment reflects continued confidence in Louisiana’s industrial strength.

“Shintech’s decision to make a $3.4 billion reinvestment after 25 years in our state speaks volumes,” Landry said. “This expansion strengthens one of the world’s leading process industry hubs and reinforces Louisiana’s role as a global industrial powerhouse.”

Shintech began operations in Louisiana in 2000 and has completed seven major projects in the state totaling about $9 billion in investment. Company officials say the new expansion will incorporate advanced technologies designed to reduce environmental emissions during production of PVC and related products.

At the same time, another major energy investment is planned for southeast Louisiana. Southern Energy Renewables announced it will invest $1.4 billion to build a green methanol and sustainable aviation fuel production facility in St. Charles Parish.

The project will convert regional wood-waste biomass into lower-carbon transportation fuels used in aviation and other industries. Officials say the facility will be among the first of its kind at a commercial scale.

The development is expected to create 120 direct jobs with an average salary of $97,267. Louisiana Economic Development estimates an additional 394 indirect jobs could be created, bringing the total potential impact to 514 jobs in the region.

Southern Energy Renewables CEO Jay Patel said Louisiana’s energy infrastructure and workforce made the state a natural choice for the project.

“With support from state and local partners, our roadmap is built to deliver fuels at an industrial scale while creating new jobs, expanding the local economy and strengthening America’s energy leadership,” Patel said.

Pre-construction planning for the St. Charles Parish facility is already underway. Construction is expected to begin in late 2027, with commercial operations anticipated in 2029.

State officials say the two projects together highlight Louisiana’s continued leadership in both traditional manufacturing and emerging energy technologies while bringing new jobs, construction activity and economic development to multiple regions of the state.

text:
The European Union is stepping up its fight against climate change. Aviation is now a key focus. New environmental rules are being applied to airlines operating in Europe. These rules aim to cut carbon emissions from flights. Airlines must now pay more for the pollution they produce. This system is part of a wider plan to reduce greenhouse gases across sectors. The changes are already affecting airline operations. They are also raising concerns across the global travel industry. For travellers, this marks the beginning of a new travel era shaped by sustainability and regulation.

Airlines Raise Concerns Over Rising Costs

Airlines are expressing strong concerns about these new policies. They believe the rules may increase operational costs significantly. Paying for carbon emissions adds financial pressure. This is especially true for long-haul carriers. Airlines argue that competitors outside Europe may not face similar rules. This creates an uneven playing field. Some carriers fear losing passengers to airlines based in less regulated regions. Industry leaders are urging policymakers to consider global alignment. Without it, European aviation could face disadvantages. These concerns highlight the tension between environmental goals and commercial realities.

Impact on Ticket Prices and Travel Planning

Travellers are likely to feel the effects soon. Airlines often pass increased costs to passengers. This means ticket prices may rise. Flights to and within Europe could become more expensive. Budget airlines may adjust their pricing strategies. Some routes may become less frequent or even disappear. Travellers may need to plan more carefully. Booking early can help secure better deals. Flexible travel dates may also reduce costs. While Europe remains a top destination, reaching it may require a bigger budget in the coming years.

Shift Towards Sustainable Aviation Practices

The new rules are part of a broader push for cleaner aviation. The European Union is encouraging the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). This type of fuel produces fewer emissions than traditional jet fuel. However, SAF is still expensive and not widely available. Airlines are investing in research and innovation. They aim to reduce their environmental impact over time. Carbon trading systems are also being used. These systems make airlines pay for their emissions. The goal is to encourage greener operations. This shift is reshaping the future of air travel.

Changing Flight Routes and Airline Strategies

Airlines are now rethinking their strategies. Some may adjust routes to reduce costs. This could lead to fewer direct flights in certain regions. Travellers might see more connecting flights instead. Airlines may also shift operations to hubs outside Europe. This helps them avoid higher regulatory costs. As a result, global travel patterns may change. Certain airports could lose transit passengers. Others may gain traffic. These adjustments are gradual but important. They reflect how environmental policies can influence global connectivity.

What Travellers Should Do Now

Travellers need to stay informed and flexible. Understanding these changes can help avoid surprises. Booking flights early is a smart move. Comparing prices across airlines is also important. Travellers should consider alternative routes and airports. Choosing off-peak travel times can reduce costs. It is also wise to check airline policies before booking. Some airlines are investing more in sustainability. Supporting such carriers can make a difference. Careful planning will help travellers manage rising costs and changing travel conditions.

A New Chapter for Global Tourism

The aviation industry is entering a new phase. Sustainability is now a top priority. Governments are taking strong action to reduce emissions. Airlines must adapt quickly to survive. Travellers are also becoming more aware of their impact. Many are choosing eco-friendly travel options. This shift is likely to continue in the coming years. The balance between affordability and sustainability will shape the future. Europe is leading this transformation. Other regions may follow similar paths. The way people travel is evolving, and change is already underway.

Conclusion: Travel Is Changing, But Opportunities Remain

The new carbon rules mark a turning point for global travel. While challenges exist, they also bring opportunities. Cleaner aviation can benefit the environment in the long term. Travellers may need to adjust their expectations. Costs may rise, and routes may change. However, Europe remains an attractive destination. Its culture, history, and landscapes continue to draw visitors. With smart planning, travellers can still enjoy meaningful journeys. The future of travel is greener, and it is arriving faster than expected.

title: Oil Shock Tightens Squeeze on Costly Green Jet Fuel - The Traveler
description:
Oil Rally Collides With Premium-Priced Sustainable Fuel The latest rise in crude oil and conventional jet fuel prices is rippling into the small but fast-growing market for sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.
In Europe, policy papers and consultancy estimates put recent indicative SAF prices in the range of about 2,000 euros per metric ton, compared with substantially lower spot prices for conventional jet fuel.
Regulatory mandates are ensuring that demand for greener jet fuel will keep rising, regardless of the price environment.
Under the European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation rules, aviation fuel suppliers at EU airports must ensure that at least 2 percent of fuel supplied from 2025 is sustainable, with the target set to increase in stages through 2050.
Airlines Pass Costs to Travelers and Rethink Networks The immediate consequence of the green fuel cost shock is beginning to show up in surcharges and ticket pricing.
text:
A renewed spike in global oil prices is pushing up the cost of greener jet fuel just as airlines face binding clean-fuel mandates, amplifying a price shock that threatens to raise ticket costs and complicate aviation’s path to net zero emissions.

Oil Rally Collides With Premium-Priced Sustainable Fuel

The latest rise in crude oil and conventional jet fuel prices is rippling into the small but fast-growing market for sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. Publicly available market assessments indicate that SAF in key mandated regions is trading at roughly two to five times the price of fossil jet fuel, a premium that becomes more painful when the underlying oil price climbs.

Industry analyses suggest that global SAF production could reach close to 2 million metric tons in 2025, still less than 1 percent of projected airline fuel consumption. Even at that modest share, forecasts compiled by aviation bodies point to billions of dollars in additional fuel costs for airlines this year and next, driven largely by the steep SAF price premium.

In Europe, policy papers and consultancy estimates put recent indicative SAF prices in the range of about 2,000 euros per metric ton, compared with substantially lower spot prices for conventional jet fuel. As oil benchmarks strengthen, that euro figure has stayed high, effectively widening the absolute cost gap per ton of fuel even if the multiple over fossil kerosene narrows slightly.

The result is a double squeeze for airlines. Higher base fuel prices increase operating costs across the board, while the requirement to blend in a small but rising share of far more expensive SAF magnifies the total fuel bill at a time when margins remain thin and competition on many routes is intense.

Regulatory mandates are ensuring that demand for greener jet fuel will keep rising, regardless of the price environment. Under the European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation rules, aviation fuel suppliers at EU airports must ensure that at least 2 percent of fuel supplied from 2025 is sustainable, with the target set to increase in stages through 2050. National and regional authorities are preparing monitoring systems and technical reports that will check whether these obligations are being met.

Parallel measures in the United Kingdom require a similar initial share of sustainable fuel, with higher targets later in the decade. Recent coverage in European business media notes that many carriers already anticipate higher operating costs as they secure supply for these mandates, particularly at hub airports where SAF availability is highest and competition for volumes is strongest.

Mandate-style policies are now spreading to Asia as well. Singapore has introduced what is described in press reports as the region’s first dedicated SAF levy, adding between a fraction of a dollar and several dozen dollars to tickets depending on cabin class and distance. The levy is earmarked to fund the purchase of sustainable fuel for flights from Changi Airport, effectively baking a green fuel cost component into ticket prices on routes across Southeast Asia and beyond.

Together, these regional initiatives mean airlines cannot fully step back from the SAF market even during an oil shock. On the contrary, the share of their fuel mix tied to greener, higher-priced product is locked in and set to grow, exposing carriers to a structural cost uplift that is difficult to offset through efficiency gains alone.

Tax Credits and Incentives Struggle to Keep Pace

On the other side of the Atlantic, the United States is attempting to cushion the cost of greener jet fuel through tax incentives introduced under the Inflation Reduction Act. Guidance published by the Internal Revenue Service explains that a dedicated sustainable aviation fuel credit is available for qualifying SAF used in fuel blends sold between the start of 2023 and the end of 2024, while a broader clean fuels production credit is scheduled to apply from 2025.

Policy analyses by environmental groups and think tanks indicate that these credits can be worth around 1.25 to 1.75 dollars per gallon for SAF that meets strict lifecycle emissions thresholds. The intention is to close part of the price gap with fossil jet fuel, encourage investment in new production capacity and stimulate long-term offtake agreements between airlines and fuel producers.

Yet as oil prices and SAF feedstock costs rise together, there are growing signs that these incentives may not fully neutralize the premium. Briefings from tax specialists highlight that the current SAF credit is temporary, and sector reports warn that uncertainty over what will replace it after 2024 could delay final investment decisions on large-scale projects in the middle of the decade.

Without a stable and predictable support framework, producers face volatile returns and may be slow to bring capacity online. That in turn keeps supply tight, limiting competition and leaving airlines dependent on a relatively small group of suppliers with strong pricing power whenever fossil fuel markets tighten.

Airlines Pass Costs to Travelers and Rethink Networks

The immediate consequence of the green fuel cost shock is beginning to show up in surcharges and ticket pricing. Public announcements by several European airline groups and logistics providers indicate that sustainable aviation fuel surcharges are being introduced or expanded on both passenger tickets and air freight shipments, often as a separate line item tied to SAF uptake.

Industry observers suggest that network planners are increasingly factoring local SAF availability and price into route decisions. Long-haul services that rely heavily on hubs in mandated markets such as the European Union or Singapore may see sharper cost increases than routes that can be scheduled through jurisdictions with weaker SAF requirements, raising questions about future competitive advantages between airlines based inside and outside strict regulatory zones.

Low cost carriers appear particularly vulnerable. Analyses published by European economic and aviation outlets argue that their business models, which rely on very low fares and high aircraft utilization, leave less room to absorb the rise in fuel costs. Any need to pass on a significant portion of the SAF premium could erode their price edge over legacy airlines, especially on routes with high rail or ferry competition.

Some carriers are exploring voluntary green fares and corporate SAF programs, offering passengers and business clients the option to pay extra for a greater share of sustainable fuel. While these schemes can help finance SAF purchases and burnish environmental credentials, market data suggests they currently cover only a fraction of total fuel needs and are sensitive to broader economic conditions and traveler willingness to pay.

Uncertain Outlook for SAF Prices as Investment Lags

Looking ahead, analysts are divided over whether the current price shock will accelerate or delay the transition to greener jet fuel. On one hand, higher fossil fuel prices can make SAF comparatively more attractive over time, especially if learning curves and economies of scale reduce production costs for advanced biofuels and synthetic e-fuels.

On the other hand, several recent market outlooks warn that high upfront costs, complex certification requirements and patchy policy support are slowing investment in new plants. International aviation organizations have cautioned that global SAF supply growth could decelerate around 2026, even as mandates and voluntary commitments continue to ratchet up, setting the stage for a prolonged period of tight supply and elevated premiums.

Travelers may feel the effects most keenly on intercontinental routes, where airlines have fewer options to substitute lower carbon transport modes. Any sustained combination of strong passenger demand, firm oil prices and costly SAF requirements is likely to keep upward pressure on long-haul ticket prices through the second half of the decade, according to recent industry forecasts.

For now, the delicate balance between energy markets, climate policy and airline economics remains in flux. What appears clear is that the interaction between oil price swings and structurally expensive green fuel is becoming a central variable in the cost of global air travel, and a critical factor in how quickly aviation can cut its climate impact without grounding growth in passenger demand.

text:
AMI Paradigm Solutions Private Limited has entered into a binding agreement to acquire the Smart World and Communication (SWC) business from L&T Technology Services Limited. The acquisition marks a significant step in building an integrated platform focused on artificial intelligence solutions for public systems and critical infrastructure.

Promoted by AM Group and Paradigm IT, AMI Paradigm Solutions aims to leverage the SWC portfolio to strengthen its capabilities in delivering AI-driven intelligence solutions. The acquired business brings expertise across smart infrastructure, communication systems, and public sector technologies, complementing AMIPS’ long-term growth strategy.

The company is developing a vertically integrated AI platform that combines clean energy, data center infrastructure, high-performance computing, software platforms, and application layers. This ecosystem is designed to support flexible consumption models, ranging from accelerator-based services to tokenized AI delivery.

Industry estimates indicate that the global market for AI in sovereign services is currently valued at approximately $25 billion and is expected to grow significantly over the next decade. Governments worldwide are increasingly adopting AI to enhance governance, improve security, and enable data-driven decision-making.

As part of its broader vision, AM Group is investing $25 billion to build a 1 GW high-performance computing hub in Uttar Pradesh. The first phase, with a capacity of around 250 MW, is currently being developed in collaboration with the Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority.

Anil Chalamalasetty, Chairman of AM Group, stated that the acquisition will help operationalize AI across mission-critical sectors such as governance, utilities, and transport. He emphasized the group’s focus on creating an efficient value chain that converts clean energy into scalable computing capabilities.

KUCHING (March 28): The Sarawak government will soon announce forms of assistance for the people to help ease the burden of the rising price of goods caused by the Middle East conflict, said Dato Sri Alexander Nanta Linggi.

Nanta, who is also Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS) secretary‑general, said the matter was disclosed by Premier Datuk Patinggi Tan Sri Abang Johari Tun Openg when speaking at the Majlis Ramah Tamah Aidilfitri organised by the Premier’s Office on Friday night.

According to Nanta, Abang Johari told those present that discussions had been held with Deputy Premier and Second Finance Minister Datuk Amar Douglas Uggah Embas, with further evaluation being carried out to ensure the aid package will truly benefit those affected.

“I greatly admire the leadership of the Sarawak Premier, Datuk Patinggi Tan Sri Abang Johari Tun Openg, who always puts the interests of the people first and never tires of listening to their complaints,” he said in a Facebook post following the event.

Elaborating further on the event, Nanta said Abang Johari in his speech also highlighted the impact of global geopolitical tensions on the global economy, citing conflicts in Venezuela and Iran which are closely tied to oil resources.

Nanta said the Premier had stressed that these developments clearly showed how reliance on fossil fuels can have a major impact on economic stability.

He also said Abang Johari mentioned that public transport initiatives, including the Autonomous Rapid Transit (ART) system, would utilise hydrogen technology in line with Sarawak’s commitment to reducing reliance on conventional energy sources.

Nanta added that a meeting would be convened soon, to be chaired by the Premier, to accelerate the adoption of SAF, with emphasis on coordinated efforts across all levels of leadership.

“This approach is not only strategic, but also important in ensuring economic stability and the well-being of the people in the long term.

“I believe that the efforts and meticulous planning of the Sarawak government will continue to ensure that the state remains sustainable, resilient and always prioritizes the welfare of the people,” he said.

On the Ramah Tamah Aidilfitri organised by the Premier’s Office, Nanta, who is also federal Works Minister, said the event provided an opportunity for him to meet and strengthen ties with Sarawak leaders, including veteran figures and members of the community from various walks of life.

title: Singapore Postpones SAF Levy as Middle East Conflict Hits Fuel - The Traveler
description:
Singapore has deferred the planned rollout of a sustainable aviation fuel levy on air passengers, as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East roils global energy markets and raises uncertainty over airline operating costs.
Singapore had been preparing to introduce a sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, levy on passengers departing from Changi Airport, with the initial rollout slated for 1 April 2026.
Middle East Conflict Disrupts Energy Markets and Flight Networks The shift in Singapore’s timetable is unfolding against a backdrop of escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted air corridors and energy flows across a region that is central to global oil and jet fuel supply.
Balancing Climate Ambitions with Cost Pressures on Travellers Singapore’s SAF levy was conceived as part of a broader climate policy package that includes national emissions reductions commitments and sector-specific targets.
Singapore’s delayed SAF levy, shaped by events far beyond its borders, underlines how closely future travel costs and climate action are now linked.
text:
Singapore has deferred the planned rollout of a sustainable aviation fuel levy on air passengers, as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East roils global energy markets and raises uncertainty over airline operating costs.

Singapore had been preparing to introduce a sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, levy on passengers departing from Changi Airport, with the initial rollout slated for 1 April 2026. Publicly available policy documents and commentaries describe the levy as a key instrument in funding the city-state’s transition toward lower-carbon air travel, supporting a national target for SAF use from the mid-2020s onward. The charge was expected to be embedded in air tickets, collected from travellers and channelled into the purchase of cleaner fuel blends for flights taking off from Singapore.

According to recent media coverage and public briefings, the new timeline has now been pushed back, with officials citing a need to reassess cost impacts in light of the deteriorating situation in the Middle East. The decision effectively pauses one of Asia’s earliest attempts at a national-level SAF passenger levy, even as other regions continue to explore similar mechanisms to decarbonise aviation.

The postponement comes on top of existing airport-related fees at Changi, such as passenger service and security charges, an aviation levy and an airport development levy, which were already slated to rise gradually over the second half of the decade to fund infrastructure expansion and hub capabilities. The SAF component was designed as an additional, dedicated contribution to climate goals rather than a replacement for those charges.

Middle East Conflict Disrupts Energy Markets and Flight Networks

The shift in Singapore’s timetable is unfolding against a backdrop of escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted air corridors and energy flows across a region that is central to global oil and jet fuel supply. Recent international reporting points to missile and drone strikes on energy and transport infrastructure, as well as intermittent closures or restrictions affecting Middle Eastern airspace. These developments have triggered flight reroutings, extended block times and higher fuel burn on affected corridors between Asia, Europe and the Gulf.

The conflict has also driven renewed volatility in crude oil benchmarks, with airlines warning in recent days that higher fuel prices are beginning to squeeze margins despite resilient passenger demand. Long-haul carriers operating through the Middle East, including those serving Singapore, face a complex mix of risk management, hedging decisions and operational adjustments as they navigate both geopolitical tensions and changing cost structures.

For Singapore, a global hub that links Southeast Asia with the Gulf, Europe and Africa, the instability raises questions about near-term fuel procurement, logistics and pricing. Public commentary within the country has highlighted concerns about exposure to oil supply disruptions, given that a significant share of imported crude and liquefied natural gas historically transits chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz. In this context, a new levy that could further raise ticket prices has become more politically and economically sensitive.

Balancing Climate Ambitions with Cost Pressures on Travellers

Singapore’s SAF levy was conceived as part of a broader climate policy package that includes national emissions reductions commitments and sector-specific targets. Analytical papers and sustainability reports note that from 2026 Singapore aims to secure a minimum share of SAF in fuel uplift at Changi, ramping up toward higher blends by 2030. The levy was one of the tools identified to help close the price gap between conventional jet fuel and cleaner, but more expensive, alternatives.

The delay does not signal a retreat from those climate ambitions, but it underscores the difficulty of sustaining green transition plans when geopolitical shocks raise baseline costs for consumers. Airlines serving Singapore are already grappling with higher operating expenses from fuel and insurance, and many have signalled caution about passing on additional charges too abruptly in a competitive market.

Travel demand through Changi has remained strong, reflecting pent-up leisure trips and robust business connectivity across Asia-Pacific. Yet the prospect of higher fares due to both market-driven fuel increases and policy-linked levies has generated debate among passengers and industry observers. Some argue that a targeted SAF charge is necessary to ensure aviation contributes fairly to decarbonisation, while others contend that implementation should be timed to avoid compounding cost-of-living pressures in periods of global instability.

Implications for Airlines, Routes and the Wider Travel Market

The postponement of the SAF levy offers airlines short-term relief from an additional surcharge on tickets sold out of Singapore, potentially easing pressure on price-sensitive routes. Carriers that had begun factoring the levy into fare structures or revenue forecasts will now need to revise their plans, even as they continue to confront elevated jet fuel costs and operational disruption tied to the Middle East conflict.

Industry analysts suggest that Singapore’s move may influence how other hubs and regulators pace their own SAF funding measures. Airports and aviation authorities worldwide are watching how passengers respond to a layered structure of charges that includes traditional infrastructure fees alongside climate-oriented levies. The experience at Changi, where hub competitiveness is central to economic strategy, will likely be studied closely by policymakers weighing similar initiatives.

For travellers, the immediate impact is that air tickets originating from Singapore will not, for now, include the additional SAF-related line item that had been signposted for the April travel period. However, this respite could prove temporary. Once energy markets stabilise and the trajectory of the Middle East conflict becomes clearer, the levy may be reintroduced, possibly with adjustments to its level or phasing to reflect lessons learned during the current crisis.

Outlook for Sustainable Aviation Policy in a Volatile World

The deferral of Singapore’s SAF levy highlights a wider challenge facing the global push for sustainable aviation: climate policies are being rolled out in an era defined by geopolitical shocks, energy insecurity and cost-of-living strains. While consensus is growing that aviation must decarbonise, the pathway to doing so in a manner that is financially and socially sustainable is far from straightforward.

Observers expect Singapore to use the pause to refine its SAF strategy, exploring options such as diversified sourcing, regional production partnerships and potential incentives for early adopters among airlines. The city-state’s position as a major refining and bunkering hub could, over time, support a scaled-up ecosystem for low-carbon fuels that reduces vulnerability to disruptions in any single region.

For the wider travel industry, the developments in Singapore serve as a reminder that environmental policy, energy security and route economics are increasingly intertwined. As conflicts in key producing regions periodically unsettle fuel markets and airspace, governments and aviation stakeholders may need to design more flexible mechanisms for funding cleaner flight technologies. Singapore’s delayed SAF levy, shaped by events far beyond its borders, underlines how closely future travel costs and climate action are now linked.

title: ICAO introduces new power bank restrictions to bolster aviation safety | New Straits Times
description:
OTTAWA: The International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), headquartered in Montreal, Canada, announced new regulations on Friday, limiting each airline passenger to a maximum of two power banks and prohibiting their recharging during flights, reported Xinhua.
According to the new specifications for lithium battery-powered power banks, which take effect immediately, flight crew members will still be permitted to carry and use the power banks in accordance with aircraft operational requirements.
ICAO said in a news release that its Dangerous Goods Panel provided expert advice to the organisation's standard-setting bodies.
Following an assessment, independent technical experts from the ICAO Air Navigation Commission endorsed the recommendations to amend the Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air.
An addendum to the technical instructions will be distributed to all 193 ICAO member states, said the organisation.
text:
OTTAWA: The International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), headquartered in Montreal, Canada, announced new regulations on Friday, limiting each airline passenger to a maximum of two power banks and prohibiting their recharging during flights, reported Xinhua.

According to the new specifications for lithium battery-powered power banks, which take effect immediately, flight crew members will still be permitted to carry and use the power banks in accordance with aircraft operational requirements.

ICAO said in a news release that its Dangerous Goods Panel provided expert advice to the organisation's standard-setting bodies.

Following an assessment, independent technical experts from the ICAO Air Navigation Commission endorsed the recommendations to amend the Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air.

The recommendations have been approved by the 36-state ICAO Council.

An addendum to the technical instructions will be distributed to all 193 ICAO member states, said the organisation.

–Bernama-Xinhua

Chilean Salmon Industry Debates Indigenous Rights Law After TV Report

A recent television investigation has prompted strong reactions from political and industry figures in Chile's salmon sector, according to SeafoodSource. The report, which aired on a national network, suggested that a Norwegian government-funded organization provides annual financial support to Indigenous communities in Chile with coastal claims. These communities are reportedly located in areas where salmon farming occurs and have the ability to stop aquaculture projects.

The broadcast has intensified existing debates surrounding a Chilean law enacted in 2008, known as the Lafkenche Law. This legislation was originally established to recognize the territorial rights of Indigenous peoples over coastal spaces. Industry stakeholders have argued that the law's application has created uncertainty and halted investments, contrary to its initial purpose. A council representing the salmon industry has called for the law to be reviewed to restore its original intent and ensure fair coexistence.

In response to the television report, a Chilean legislative committee president described the allegations as extremely serious and stated that the matter would be raised with a government minister. He also mentioned the potential for advancing legislation that would require non-governmental organizations to disclose their funding sources more transparently. Other lawmakers urged the foreign ministry to verify the accusations and called for modifications to the law, with the possibility of sanctions if the claims are confirmed.

A representative of the Norwegian organization involved stated that the group did not suggest or promote the Chilean law, describing its support for the Indigenous communities as coincidental. Meanwhile, a leader from an Indigenous group emphasized that peaceful coexistence with salmon farmers is possible, noting that a significant portion of existing concessions in one region remain unused and calling for sustainable solutions.

The television report also contextualized the relationship between Chile and Norway, identifying them as the world's two leading salmon producers. It cited a Chilean academic who noted that a severe virus outbreak in 2007, which originated from Norway, significantly impacted Chile's industry. “Reviewing the EU ETS offers a critical opportunity to refocus efforts on cost-effective emission reductions.
IATA said aviation, as a global industry, should remain subject to a single international market-based mechanism under the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, known as CORSIA.

text:
The European Union should review its emissions trading system to avoid undermining the competitiveness of its aviation sector as airlines decarbonise, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said on Monday.

It also urged Brussels to align more closely with global rules and channel more carbon revenues back into the industry.

The airline body said the review of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) should focus on four areas.

These include the full implementation of the global CORSIA carbon scheme for all international flights, the introduction of a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) book-and-claim mechanism, greater reinvestment of ETS revenues into aviation decarbonisation, and a broader effort to balance climate ambition with the sector’s economic resilience.

Its call comes as concerns grow in Europe over the impact of high energy costs, complex regulation and weak investment on the bloc’s competitiveness, a debate that has intensified following the findings of Mario Draghi’s report on Europe’s economic resilience.

“European aviation policy must bolster competitiveness as it advances decarbonisation,” IATA Director General Willie Walsh said.

“Reviewing the EU ETS offers a critical opportunity to refocus efforts on cost-effective emission reductions. The priority must be the full implementation of CORSIA, the reinvestment of EU ETS revenues into SAF and other credible decarbonisation solutions, and the elimination of overlapping measures that add cost and complexity without environmental gain,” he added.

He said this would help protect European air connectivity, which he described as a strategic asset underpinning trade, commerce and EU integration, at a time of wider economic strain and geopolitical uncertainty.

IATA said aviation, as a global industry, should remain subject to a single international market-based mechanism under the International Civil Aviation Organisation’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, known as CORSIA.

According to the association, the EU should apply CORSIA fully to all international flights, including intra-EEA routes, rather than layering regional measures on top of the global framework.

It warned that overlapping rules create extra costs and administrative burdens without delivering additional environmental benefits, while also risking fragmentation of the regulatory system.

The association also called for the EU to introduce purchase-based claiming for sustainable aviation fuel under the EU ETS through a so-called book-and-claim system. Such a mechanism would allow airlines to claim the environmental benefits of SAF based on their purchases, regardless of where the fuel is physically uplifted.

IATA said this would improve investment certainty, support a more transparent SAF market and help create a more level playing field for carriers across Europe, including those operating far from major fuel hubs.

It added that this would require targeted amendments to the ETS directive, as well as an expanded Union Database capable of tracking both the physical movement of SAF and its environmental attributes.

At the same time, the body said Brussels should return a greater share of aviation’s ETS contributions to the sector to support the transition to cleaner operations, particularly as the financial burden has increased since the 2024 phase-out of free allowances.

It said the existing SAF Allowance scheme covers only a small share of expected demand, estimated at around 4 to 5 per cent of the industry’s total allowance needs between 2026 and 2030, and argued that both its size and duration should be expanded.

Citing the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan, IATA said investment needs to meet the EU’s SAF targets were estimated at between 57 billion euros and 67 billion euros by 2035, rising to between 268 billion euros and 376 billion euros by 2050.

The aviation sector is expected to surrender nearly 330 million allowances between 2026 and 2030, generating billions of euros in revenues for member states, it added, but said only limited amounts had so far been reinvested through the EU Innovation Fund.

Future support, it said, should focus on emerging SAF technologies, helping airlines absorb the high cost of early-stage solutions and restoring free allowances to protect competitiveness and prevent investment from being diverted away from green projects.

More broadly, IATA said the EU needed to avoid a sharp rise in compliance costs at a time when geopolitical instability is already putting pressure on connectivity and passenger choice.

“A sudden increase in compliance costs, especially in a fragile geopolitical and economic context, risks weakening connectivity, reducing consumer choice, and diverting resources away from decarbonisation investments,” it said.

Finally, IATA said the EU ETS could still play an important role in aviation’s transition, but only if climate policy remains grounded in scientific evidence, aligned with international standards and designed in a way that does not impose disproportionate costs on airlines and passengers.

text:
Austrian Airlines is strengthening its push toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) adoption by improving fuel efficiency through a shark skin-inspired technology on its long-haul aircraft, Travel and Tour World reported.

The airline has applied AeroShark film to its Boeing 777-200ER fleet, helping reduce drag and lower fuel consumption. The modification, tested on four aircraft, has resulted in annual savings of about 930 tonnes of fuel and a reduction of nearly 3,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.

The AeroShark technology, developed by Lufthansa Technik and BASF, uses a surface design inspired by shark skin to minimise friction between the aircraft and surrounding air, improving overall efficiency.

The film has been applied to around 830 square metres of each aircraft, covering key sections of the fuselage and engine areas. The rollout was carried out after receiving approval from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency.

According to the airline, the emissions reduction achieved through the technology is comparable to eliminating the carbon output of around 20 transatlantic flights.

The initiative forms part of the airline’s broader strategy to cut emissions and prepare for greater use of SAF in the future. By reducing overall fuel consumption, the airline aims to make the transition to cleaner fuels more effective and economically viable.

Officials said the airline will continue to monitor the performance of the modified aircraft and explore expanding similar solutions across its fleet, as the aviation sector looks for ways to balance efficiency with environmental responsibility.

title: Summit Sold Its Midwest Pipeline as a Carbon Solution. Now, It'll Be Used for Fossil Fuels.
authors: Derek Harrison, Anika Jane Beamer, Kiley Price
description:
In the background of this eminent domain standoff, Iowa-based Summit Carbon Solutions, the company behind the pipeline, has quietly shifted its focus from carbon sequestration to fossil fuel extraction.
The Climate Pitch Summit Carbon Solutions is a subsidiary of the Iowa-based private equity firm Summit Agricultural Group, which owns nearly 14,000 acres of farmland in the state.
When Summit first filed a petition to construct its “Midwest Carbon Express” pipeline with the Iowa Utilities Commission, it was 2021, the first year of the climate-focused Biden administration.

text:
For four years, battles over private property rights have gridlocked state legislatures across the Midwest and stalled plans for a pipeline to transport liquified carbon dioxide from ethanol plants in the region.

In the background of this eminent domain standoff, Iowa-based Summit Carbon Solutions, the company behind the pipeline, has quietly shifted its focus from carbon sequestration to fossil fuel extraction.

Summit now says its pipeline will be used to drive domestic oil and gas production in a process known as enhanced oil recovery (EOR), which injects CO2 gas into wells. The gas mixes with oil in the rock pores to produce a thinner, easier-to-pump fluid, potentially doubling the amount of oil that can be extracted from a reservoir.

Just a few years ago, Summit’s website stated that the project wouldn’t be used for EOR. Instead, it advertised the pipeline as a way to cut emissions through underground sequestration. Soon after, Summit heralded it as a critical step in developing lower-carbon sustainable aviation fuel.

But as the company struggles to advance its pipeline out of a permitting quagmire and faces legal battles over property rights in Iowa, North Dakota and South Dakota, it finds itself in a starkly different energy market and political landscape.

The company’s messaging now parallels President Donald Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” policies, which seek to bolster American fossil fuel production while reversing progress on renewable energy and loosening restrictions on the greenhouse gas pollution damaging the climate.

Opponents of the pipeline have criticized Summit’s shift, arguing that the company will say whatever it takes to get the project over the finish line.

“It’s just whatever’s convenient for them in the moment,” said Jess Mazour, the conservation coordinator for the Iowa Chapter of the Sierra Club.

In late 2024, the organization filed a lawsuit challenging the Iowa Utilities Commission’s approval of Summit’s permit.

Summit did not respond to repeated email and phone requests for comment on the company’s pivot.

The Climate Pitch

Summit Carbon Solutions is a subsidiary of the Iowa-based private equity firm Summit Agricultural Group, which owns nearly 14,000 acres of farmland in the state. Both companies are founded and chaired by Iowa’s Bruce Rastetter, an agribusiness entrepreneur known for his frequent donations to state and federal Republican candidates and campaigns.

When Summit first filed a petition to construct its “Midwest Carbon Express” pipeline with the Iowa Utilities Commission, it was 2021, the first year of the climate-focused Biden administration. The company proposed transporting liquified CO2 from ethanol plants in the state to be stored underground in North Dakota.

At the time, the company’s argument for the pipeline was two-pronged: Carbon capture technology would cut greenhouse gas emissions and open new, lower-carbon fuel markets for corn and ethanol, boosting a struggling Midwest farm economy.

Using the Internet Archive, a nonprofit digital library, Inside Climate News analyzed how Summit’s language on the project website evolved over time.

In 2021, the site urgently called for net-zero CO2 emissions by 2050 and told visitors that “a dramatic increase in carbon capture and storage” would be critical to achieving net-zero and staying within 1.5 degrees Celsius of global warming, a goal set in the Paris Agreement.

Through 2023, Summit continued to emphasize carbon neutrality, estimating that the project would prevent the release of 12 million metric tons of CO2 to the atmosphere every year.

For years, Summit advertised that the pipeline would have an annual emissions-reduction impact equivalent to taking 2.6 million vehicles off the road. In fact, the project arose largely out of a need to stay competitive in a changing automotive industry.

Rising U.S. demand for electric vehicles after 2018 put the squeeze on an already plateauing ethanol industry, the final destination for some 35 percent of all U.S. corn grown in 2025, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

From the beginning of the pipeline project, Summit argued that lowering ethanol’s carbon index was essential to keeping the fuel competitive in places with renewable fuel standards and protecting corn demand for farmers already struggling to make a profit. For a while, Summit wanted to compete in the sustainable aviation fuel market, which produces lower-emission jet fuel from low-carbon ethanol.

In 2023, Summit Agricultural Group launched another subsidiary, Summit Next Gen, and announced plans to develop the world’s largest ethanol-to-sustainable aviation fuel plant in Texas’ Port Houston. The company purchased a 60-acre site for the plant in September 2024 but have announced no updates about the project since then.

Lucrative Business

While Summit advertised its pipeline as a way for corn growers to tap the pocketbooks of increasingly climate-conscious consumers and transportation sectors, the approach also made sense for the company’s bottom line.

The federal government has long offered generous tax credits for carbon capture and storage technology in an effort to cut greenhouse gas emissions and jump-start development of the expensive and relatively unproven infrastructure.

Congress significantly expanded the tax credit for carbon sequestration in 2018 and again in 2022, offering up to $85 per metric ton of CO2 captured and permanently stored. Carbon captured for use in enhanced oil recovery also qualified for tax credits—though slightly smaller ones, up to $65 per metric ton.

For years, Summit was adamant that it would not pursue those smaller tax incentives. A “Get The Facts” page on Summit’s website told visitors from late 2022 through mid-2024 that the “Summit Carbon Solutions project will not be used for enhanced oil recovery.” Instead, at that time, the company emphasized the pipeline’s importance in reducing carbon emissions and limiting global warming.

Summit’s public-facing climate pitch was strategic, said Brian Jorde, a lawyer representing Midwest landowners in legal challenges to Summit’s permit applications. “They leaned into sequestration,” he said. “But they only designed that business model because that was the most lucrative at the time.”

In fact, after the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act beefed-up tax incentives for carbon capture, Summit signed deals to add 25 ethanol facilities to its proposed pipeline, bringing the total metric tons of CO2 to be transported each year to 16 million. All that CO2 under contract meant that Summit stood to recover as much as $1.5 billion in potential tax credits each year.

Abandoning Decarbonization

Early in Trump’s second term, however, the carbon conversation took a turn.

In a barrage of attacks on existing environmental and climate policy, Trump gutted incentives for renewable energy projects, invested in carbon-intensive energy sources like coal and oil, opened swaths of public land to mining and drilling, and reversed a key federal finding that linked greenhouse gas emissions to human health.

While simultaneously halting government action on what he’s called “the climate hoax” and kneecapping development of affordable renewables like solar and wind, Trump says he wants to usher in an era of American “energy dominance.”

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Trump’s sweeping One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 also increased tax incentives for CO2 emissions captured and used in enhanced oil recovery. Now, whether a project captures carbon for permanent storage or to drive fossil fuel production, it receives the same credits.

In a complete departure from plans made just a few years ago, Summit has been quick to adapt to the new political realities. Early this year, the company scrubbed the phrases “climate change” and “global warming” from its website.

Instead, a new page announces Summit’s plans to become “the critical CO2 supply artery for America’s most prolific oil and gas basins,” the Powder River Basin in Montana and Wyoming, the Bakken Formation spanning parts of North Dakota and Montana and the Permian Basin of Texas and New Mexico.

These regions will depend on CO2 to sustain oil and gas production in the future, Summit wrote, and the pipeline will support “America’s long-term goal of energy dominance.”

For several years, Kathy Stockdale has driven over an hour from her home in Iowa Falls to the state Capitol every week to demand that lawmakers ban the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines statewide. She bakes cookies for the lawmakers; they’re more likely to interact with the anti-pipeline advocates that way, she says.

In mid-January, Stockdale spoke with Rastetter, Summit’s CEO, who was visiting the Capitol with Jake Ketzner, a lobbyist for the company. Rastetter told Stockdale, who recorded the conversation, that Summit planned to use the carbon pipeline for both direct storage and enhanced oil recovery.

“Where are you planning on using it for enhanced oil recovery?” Stockdale asked during the conversation.

Both Rastetter and Ketzner responded, “Wyoming.”

Summit did not respond to questions from Inside Climate News about that conversation.

The company’s embrace of enhanced oil recovery is likely an economic decision made in response to Trump’s modification of federal tax credits, said Matt Fry, director of the ​​Center for Energy Regulation and Policy Analysis at the University of Wyoming and former policy and technical director at the Great Plains Institute, where he supported carbon capture, utilization and storage projects in the region.

“I think the new ‘energy dominance’ policy, if you will, probably plays a little bit into [Summit’s] new motivation.”

— Matt Fry, ​​Center for Energy Regulation and Policy Analysis

Though Summit emphasized permanent carbon storage in the project’s early years, EOR was never off the table for its executives, Fry said.

“If you’ve ever listened to them talk at conferences, or read some of their old interviews, they never said that they were opposed to it. They always said that it was an option and the market would kind of dictate things,” he said.

The tax credits that offer equal incentives for enhanced oil recovery and permanent storage projects have altered the market, said Fry. “I think the new ‘energy dominance’ policy, if you will, probably plays a little bit into [Summit’s] new motivation,” he said.

Fry doesn’t see Summit backing away from enhanced oil recovery now. Oil and gas are critical to making a dizzying array of everyday and specialty products, not just fuel for the transportation sector. He doesn’t see the drilling industry going away.

And if fossil fuel production is to continue, demand for CO2-enhanced oil recovery will likely grow as well, Fry said. As old basins produce less and less oil with traditional extraction technology, “I think we’re going to have to deploy EOR, from a production perspective,” he said. “I think that the market’s going to drive it.”

Jorde, the lawyer representing landowners, thinks that Summit in fact planned to pursue EOR from the outset of the pipeline, but that admitting so “wouldn’t have been the best path to getting the project approved.”

“Permission to Explore All Options”

While Summit changed their story online, a series of permitting roadblocks on the ground may have also propelled the pivot.

South Dakota banned the use of eminent domain for siting carbon pipelines in 2025, creating a hurdle in the Summit pipeline’s planned route to North Dakota. Further complicating the terrain, this month a North Dakota judge revoked a permit from Summit that would have allowed it to store CO2 underground in the state.

Those decisions, in turn, are imperiling Summit’s permit in Iowa which binds the pipeline to its original route. Summit petitioned the Iowa Utilities Commission in September 2025 to amend the terms of its permit and remove mentions of a specific route or destination.

Summit is now considering destinations in Nebraska, Wyoming, Colorado and Kansas, Bret Dublinske, an attorney for the company, said in an Iowa district court hearing in September. “We’re asking for permission to explore all options,” he said.

Jorde does not believe the permit can be altered so substantially. “This obvious pivot … should completely invalidate that application,” Jorde said. “The Iowa Utilities Commission should just take that action without any motion, simply nullify the permit and then force them to start over and tell us who they really are once and for all.”

In a cease-and-desist letter that Summit Carbon Solutions sent to the Sierra Club’s Mazour in late 2024 over comments she’d made to members of the press, the company stated that $1 billion had already been invested in the project. Summit did not respond to multiple requests for an updated version of that figure.

Mazour isn’t sure the solution is as simple as Summit being forthright about plans for the pipeline.

“I don’t even know if they know what they’re going to do,” said Mazour. “I think they’re just trying to put all the cards out on the table and figure out which one might work and then go with that one.”

text:
The operators of Sullom Voe Terminal (SVT) have announced plans to start work on an e-methanol facility producing sustainable marine and aviation fuels.

EnQuest said in its end of year report for 2025, published this week, that its subsidiary Veri Energy was expected to begin “front-end engineering and design” for the facility this year.

Veri launched a major initiative to investigate e-fuel production plans at SVT last year, with the aim of “harnessing Shetland’s exceptional wind resource” as part of wider ambitions to transform the terminal into a future energy hub.

The new financial report states that support from Aberdeen’s Net Zero Technology Centre, through its Energy Hubs project, had enabled development of an “advanced operating model for future e-fuel facilities”.

Following analysis of options, Veri said it would prioritise the development of an e-methanol facility.

The production of e-fuels, including e-methanol, involves the use of green hydrogen, produced from water via electrolysis powered by renewable energy.

At SVT it would be achieved using a 50MW hydrogen plant, powered using wind energy.

The green hydrogen would then combined with carbon dioxide, derived from a separate carbon capture process, to produce a synthetic gas, which would then be refined into hydrocarbon fuels that can replace jet fuel.

EnQuest’s report said e‐methanol had been selected due to its “strong applicability for marine decarbonisation and its role as a key feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel via methanol‐to‐jet technology”.

The company said work would also take place this year to explore the expansion into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production.

The UK government has introduced a sustainable aviation fuel mandate requiring 10 per cent of fuel used by the aviation industry to be SAF by 2030, growing to 22 per cent by 2040.

Speaking previously about the e-fuel project, Veri chief executive Gavin Templeton said the company’s focus was on unlocking Scotland’s potential to produce low-carbon fuels by “harnessing Shetland’s exceptional wind resource to enhance long-term energy resilience”.

“Repurposing the industrial footprint at Sullom Voe allows us to retain and redeploy highly skilled engineering jobs, work hand in hand with the local community, and deliver industrial decarbonisation in a way that’s both responsible and enduring,” he added.

“If successful, this will serve as a scalable model for gigawatt-level low-carbon fuel production - paving the way to decarbonise homes, businesses and infrastructure across the country.”

Since 2023, Veri has been exploring a range of initiatives to repurposing potential of SVT into a leading energy hub for future fuels and other energy transition opportunities.

The company is seeking to develop a means to transport and permanently store up to 10 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, taken from emitters in the UK and Europe.

The captured carbon dioxide would be taken by ship to SVT from where it will be transported via repurposed pipelines for permanent storage in depleted oil and gas reservoirs.

title: EPA finalizes robust 2026, 2027 RFS RVOs | Ethanol Producer Magazine
description:
The U.S. EPA on March 27 finalized the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard renewable volume obligations (RVOs) at levels higher than originally proposed.
For 2026, the nested RVOs include 1.36 billion cellulosic RINs, 8.86 billion biomass-based diesel RINs, and 10.82 billion advanced biofuel RINs.
The nested RVOs for 2027 increase to 1.43 billion cellulosic RINs, 8.95 billion biomass-based diesel RINs, and 10.98 billion advanced biofuel RINs.
For 2027, the SRE reallocation volume has been finalized at 1.04 billion RINs, including 340 million advanced biofuel RINs and 250 million biomass-based diesel RINs.
The agency in mid-2023 finalized the 2025 cellulosic ROV at 1.38 billion RINs and in June 2025 proposed to reduce the 2025 cellulosic RVO to 1.19 billion RINs.
text:
The U.S. EPA on March 27 finalized the 2026 and 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard renewable volume obligations (RVOs) at levels higher than originally proposed. The increase is primarily attributed to the decision to delay the implementation of provisions that penalize foreign produced fuels and feedstocks until at least 2028. The rule also reallocates 70% of volumes waived through small refinery exemptions (SREs) and eliminates electricity from the RFS program.

The EPA in June 2025 released a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to set 2026 and 2027 RVOs and make other fundamental changes to the RFS program, including a proposal to strip renewable electricity from the program. The NPRM also included provisions that aim to incentivize the use of domestic feedstocks and domestically produced biofuel by reducing the quantity of renewable identification numbers (RIN) generated for foreign fuels and fuels made from imported feedstocks by 50%, referred to by the agency as its “import RIN reduction” (IRR) policy. A supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking (SNPRM) released in September 2025 sought public input on the potential reallocation of waived SRE volumes. The agency has now taken final action on both proposals, which the agency refers to as the “Set 2” rulemaking.

The EPA has finalized the RVO for total renewable fuels at 25.82 billion renewable identification numbers (RINs) in 2026 and 25.98 billion RINs in 2027, up from the respective volumes of 24.02 billion RINs and 24.46 billion RINs included in the proposed rule released in June 2025. The EPA primarily attributed the higher finalized RVO volumes to its decision to delay implementation of the IRR policy until 2028 or later, noting that while although the RIN requirements are higher, the RVOs in terms of fuel volumes are largely unchanged.

For 2026, the nested RVOs include 1.36 billion cellulosic RINs, 8.86 billion biomass-based diesel RINs, and 10.82 billion advanced biofuel RINs. The nested RVOs for 2027 increase to 1.43 billion cellulosic RINs, 8.95 billion biomass-based diesel RINs, and 10.98 billion advanced biofuel RINs. The implied RVO for corn-based ethanol was maintained at 15 billion gallons for both years.

The EPA is also finalizing a 70% partial reallocation of the 2023-2025 RVOs waived via the SRE program for 2026 and 2027. “This approach will balance a number of factors that come into play when considering volume requirements and the impacts of SREs, including protecting biofuel demand while maintaining a stable and functioning credit market,” the agency said in a statement.

The SRE reallocation volume for 2026 has been set at approximately 990 million RINs, including 280 million advanced biofuel RINs and 210 million biomass-based diesel RINs. For 2027, the SRE reallocation volume has been finalized at 1.04 billion RINs, including 340 million advanced biofuel RINs and 250 million biomass-based diesel RINs.

As a result, the total applicable RVO for 2026 is 26.81 billion RINs, including the nested volumes of 11.1 billion advanced biofuel RINs, 9.07 billion biomass-based diesel RINs and 1.36 billion cellulosic RINs. For 2028, the total applicable RVO has been finalized at 27.02 billion RINs, including the nested volumes of 11.32 billion advanced biofuel RINs, 9.2 billion biomass-based diesel RINs, and 1.43 billion cellulosic biofuel RINs.

The EPA also finalized a proposal to reduce the 2025 cellulosic RVO, but at a lesser rate than proposed last June. The agency in mid-2023 finalized the 2025 cellulosic ROV at 1.38 billion RINs and in June 2025 proposed to reduce the 2025 cellulosic RVO to 1.19 billion RINs. The agency, however, has finalized the reduction at 1.21 billion RINs.

The EPA’s June 2025 proposal included provisions aimed at boosting domestic biofuel production by limiting the ability for imported fuels and feedstocks to participate in the RFS. Under the proposal foreign biofuels and feedstocks would only generate 50% of the RIN value relative to domestic biofuels and feedstocks.

Within the final rule, the EPA explains it has elected not to finalize this import RIN reduction (IRR) policy as part of the “Set 2" rule, citing the need for more time to “successfully establish and implement IRR provisions.” Specifically, the EPA said commenters indicated the proposed IRR provisions “could result in significant changes to the supply of the renewable fuels and feedstocks to U.S. markets and these changes could be disruptive without sufficient lead time for the market to prepare and make necessary adjustments—including leading to increase in gasoline and diesel prices.”

The agency said it intends “to establish IRR provisions that will take effect beginning in the 2028 compliance year or shortly thereafter.” According to the rule, the EPA is currently considering the next steps associated with the IRR proposal and will communicate with stakeholders as it considers its plans.

The EPA followed through with a proposal to strip electricity, or eRINs, from the RFS. The agency had taken steps in recent years to roll electricity into the RFS program but ultimately failed to approve a single eRIN pathway. The final rule issued March 27 formally removes “renewable electricity” from the RFS program.

The final rule also includes a variety of other regulatory changes to the RFS program, including specifying new equivalence values for renewable diesel, naphtha and jet fuel; updating RIN generation and assignment provisions; clarifying that RINs cannot be generated for renewable fuel that is used for process heat or electricity generation; changing the percentage standards equations, including specifying the biobased diesel standard in RINs rather than physical gallons; updating existing renewable fuel pathways and adding new ones; adding definitions for terms used throughout the regulations and updating other definitions; adding a joint and several liability provision applicable to importers of renewable fuel; revising compliance and registration provisions, including clarifying that small refineries that receive an exemption from their RFS obligations must stills submit an annual compliance report; clarifying certain requirements for biodiesel and renewable diesel and other minor changes and technical corrections.

For biogas specifically, the rule includes language clarifying what constitutes a batch of renewable natural gas (RNG); clarifying the requirements for the generation, assignment and separation of RINs for RNG; clarifying registration requirements for biogas producers, RNG producers and RNG RIN separators; and numerous clarifications, corrections and consistency edits to the biogas regulations.

The Renewable Fuels Association is welcoming the 2026 and 2027 RVOs. “At a time when American consumers are looking for relief at the pump and hard-hit farmers are looking for new demand opportunities, we commend EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and President Donald Trump for delivering robust RFS volume requirements for 2026 and 2027,” said Geoff Cooper, president and CEO of the RFA. “The final rule locks in the highest-ever renewable fuel volume obligations and provides clarity for farmers, ethanol producers, oil refiners, and fuel distributors alike. Today’s action by EPA and the White House will boost the farm economy, strengthen American energy security, and reduce fuel prices for hardworking families. We applaud the Trump administration for recognizing the important role renewable fuels and agriculture can play in meeting our nation’s energy dominance objectives.”

The American Coalition for Ethanol is also applauding the final RVOs. “Congress intended year-to-year renewable fuel blending to increase under the RFS and today’s announcement with the highest-ever volume obligations helps fulfill their intention,” said Brian Jennings, CEO of ACE. “ We’ve consistently advocated for strong final blending obligations for 2026 and 2027 reflecting the full potential of the RFS and ensuring small refinery exemptions (SREs) do not erode demand for renewable fuels. It is critical that EPA set blending requirements at levels that fully account for any SREs granted. Failing to do so risks undermining the intent of the RFS by allowing obligated parties to rely on surplus renewable identification numbers (RINs) rather than driving actual blending and use of renewable fuels.

“The integrity of the RFS depends on ensuring volume obligations translate into real-world demand,” he added. “Any gap between required volumes and actual blending undermines the program and creates uncertainty for ethanol producers, farmers, and rural communities.

“Importantly, EPA has the authority to set volumes that require more than 15 billion gallons of conventional biofuels annually. We would encourage EPA to seriously consider higher volumes next year to account for any negative impact from SRE gallons not being fully reallocated and for potential E15 increases.

“When properly implemented, the RFS strengthens U.S. energy security, supports America’s farmers and rural communities, saves consumers money at the pump, and cleans the air for everyone,” Jennings continued. “ACE remains committed to working with EPA and the Administration to ensure the program delivers on these goals, including as the Agency begins developing future volume requirements for 2028 and beyond.”

Growth Energy is celebrating the historic RVOs and SRE reallocation. “With this rulemaking, EPA and the administration are reinforcing their unwavering support for American-made biofuels and sending a strong signal about the continued role biofuels like ethanol will play in delivering American energy dominance and greater prosperity to the heartland,” said Emily Skor, CEO of Growth Energy. “We commend President Trump, EPA Administrator Zeldin, and USDA Secretary Rollins for working together to finalize this historic, growth-oriented proposal, which opens the market for more than 15 billion gallons of conventional biofuel in 2026 and 2027.

“USDA also deserves our industry’s thanks for its advocacy on behalf of American farmers—the agency worked tirelessly to ensure that the final RVOs reflected the President’s agenda for unleashing American energy and restoring prosperity to rural America,” she added.” With so many farm families struggling to make ends meet, we must take every opportunity to build reliable, domestic markets for American agriculture.

“Furthermore, we applaud EPA for making the decision to reallocate 70% of all gallons lost to 2023-2025 SREs. This provides clarity and predictability across the liquid fuel supply chain, while guaranteeing that the new markets promised to American farmers and biofuel producers as part of the RVOs are not destroyed by costly exemptions.

“We are grateful to President Trump and his administration for its steadfast support for homegrown biofuels, and for setting a new high watermark for American ethanol,” Skor continued. “We look forward to continuing our work with EPA and Congressional champions as we continue to find ways to strengthen domestic energy security and open new market opportunities for U.S. farmers and rural communities.”

Clean Fuels Alliance America said the final rule provides much needed certainty for biodiesel and renewable diesel producers. “The entire U.S. clean fuel industry – from farmers and feedstock providers to fuel customers – is grateful to see this rule finalized,” said Kurt Kovarik, vice president of federal affairs at Clean Fuels. “U.S. biodiesel, renewable diesel, and SAF producers are eager to get to work and bring the 7 billion gallons of existing production capacity up to speed to meet 10% or more of America’s demand for diesel fuel.”

“The robust biomass-based diesel volumes set in this rule support America’s farmers and consumers,” Kovarik continued. “Biodiesel and renewable diesel represent 10% of the value of every bushel of U.S.-grown soybeans, contributing to President Trump’s desire for American energy dominance and domestic market demand for agriculture commodities. American farmers and other feedstock providers are eager for the growing domestic clean fuel market to drive value in agriculture, along with economic growth and job creation in rural communities. American consumers are desperate for secure, affordable domestic energy. Today’s rule is a clear win for the nation’s energy security.”

The RNG Coalition praised the EPA’s decision to finalize the cellulosic RVOs at levels higher than originally proposed. “The final rule is certainly an improvement over the agency’s Set 2 proposal," said Johannes Escudero, founder and CEO of the RNG Coalition. "The RNG COALITION will continue to urge EPA to administer a growth-oriented program as envisioned by Congress.

“The RNG industry in the U.S. has grown substantially over the last decade due in part to a strong RFS,” he added. “The program is critical to supporting significant investment across American communities and growing volumes of clean fuel. The current instability in global energy markets means the RFS has a key role to play in buttressing U.S. fuel supply and energy security.

"With hundreds of facilities under construction, we stand ready to continue supplying increasing volumes of American alternative fuels through the horizon of Set 2.0 and beyond,” Escudero continued.

The American Biogas Council said the rule constrains domestic fuel production and undercuts opportunities for farmers. EPA’s final rule fails to represent real-world biogas growth, which will constrain markets. “The action especially undercuts opportunities for livestock farmers, impeding one of the most reliable ways farmers can keep pace in a low-margin agriculture industry, and contribute to America’s energy dominance,” said Patrick Serfass, executive director of the ABC.

“In this set of fuel targets for 2026 and 2027, the agency diverged from longstanding methods and abandoned statutory guidelines when they estimated D3 RIN volumes on projected renewable natural gas (RNG) end-use constraints rather than what the U.S. biogas industry can produce – and even with this new approach, the agency has also significantly underestimated real-world demand,” Serfass continued. “This approach looks to constrain domestic, renewable fuel production, a foundation of RFS goals, instead of supporting U.S. fuel industries which recycle organic residues, and more fully utilize American crops.”

A full copy of the final “Set 2” rule is available on the EPA website.
